questions.question: Describe the bystander effect and explain why the presence of others reduces helping behaviour.

points.text: The bystander effect: more bystanders = less helping. Reasons: diffusion of responsibility, pluralistic ignorance (nobody else seems concerned), and audience inhibition (fear of looking foolish). Latane & Darley's decision-making model: notice -> interpret -> take responsibility -> decide how to help -> implement help.

questions.question: Evaluate whether true altruism exists, using psychological research.

points.text: True altruism debate: Cialdini's negative state relief model argues that helping reduces our own distress - so all helping is selfish. Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis argues that empathy motivates genuine altruism. Evidence: high-empathy people help even when they can easily escape the situation.

questions.question: Explain how the cost-reward model accounts for prosocial behaviour and evaluate its limitations.

points.text: The cost-reward model explains helping as rational calculation. Strengths: supported by research. Limitations: ignores emotional responses (people often help instinctively), cannot explain impulsive heroism, assumes people always act rationally in emergencies.

points.text: A grade 9 response will: describe the bystander effect with Latane & Darley's research; explain mechanisms (diffusion of responsibility, pluralistic ignorance, audience inhibition); evaluate using real-world evidence; consider alternative explanations; conclude: the bystander effect is well-established but real emergencies involve more complex processes than lab studies capture.
